Everyone loves Arma 3, right? Well I don't. I bought Operation Flashpoint when it was brand new and I played it alot for several years. The game had its fair share of bugs, but all in all it was very enjoyable. The graphics were not top notch and neither were the phycisc or mechanics, but still it made for a challenging and rewarding gaming experience. Even more so, as I was able to download several mods (like the Finnish Winter war) which further extended the experience. But I eventually stopped playing the game and practically forgot about it. Years later, for a bargain price I picked up a single module for Arma II, but it was very limited and I quickly uninstalled it again. Then I begun reading good things about Arma III. And at the after Christmas sales 2020, I decided to have a go. This is my verdict. Please notice that I am discussing the single player campaign, which is the reason why I bought the game, as I'm not really into this type of multiplayer gaming:

Arma III is not a very good game. Strangely enough, it seems to have preserved many of the pathfinding bugs from Operation Flashpoint, which is quite an achievement, considering 20 years have passed. I have had soldiers refusing to get into cars or to follow me, because they are stopped by invisible barriers. Or they make a detour around the village, before they manage to fall in line. Further more, the game is not fair in any way. You can basically forget about stealth all together, because the AI-troopers have ESP-capabilities to let them know whenever you are sneaking up on them. They will then proceed to insta-kill you more often than not. I also find it practically impossible to hit (let alone see) anything beyond about 100 meters or so (and I would like to point out that I'm a decent marksman IRL). Every mission in the single player campaign takes place at running speed and your comrades will simply run away from you all the time, while you are tagging along with your (virtual) lungs about to explode. Also you are constantly bombarded with cryptic instructions, which will make you run off in the wrong direction or just stand about, looking for a clue, until enemy patrols converge on your position. And you can just forget about taking cover or hiding. Those guys are blood hounds.

So after 15 hours of play, I have progressed about 5 missions and had my bejeebies handed to me about 50 times. This is not very enjoyable at all. And then comes a mission where you are supposed to set up a drone and fly it over the enemy positions to look for their artillery position. Well, good luck with that! Even after finding the drone itself, I couldn't deploy it because I need some more equipment, which I havn't even figured out what or where it is, or if I was supposed to pack it in my kit before the mission started. So, i just decided to leave the campaign for awhile. And so I remembered that there is also a very capable mission creater. And how did that pan out?

Well, it didn't. The toolbox itself is very nice, though you will have to experiment alot, because there are no instructions. And when you finally succeed in getting some things to run, you notice that you can't play your scenario anyway. Because you only have access to the limited amount of the stuff that is in the game. So a lot of the weapons and vehicles in the creation tool are just placeholders for DLC-content which you will have to pay a hefty ammount of cash for. This is not like it was 20 years ago!

So, basically, what you get for the general game license is a limited multiplayer experience, a completely messed up and broken singleplayer campaign, and a mission creator lacking any kind of instructions. Not what I was expecting after 20 years of development.

And then, just to kick you in the privates, the game crashes my computer EVERY TIME I close the application...
Very Fun 10/10 no bugs at all :)
Its hard to get into the game and overall isnt new user friendly. Bad performance overall

Arma 3 is a weird game to review, in the sense that a traditionally structured evaluation isn't really possible. That's because of the game's greatest strength is its unparalleled flexibility - it can be almost anything you want. Local and server mods can transform a rigid and serious military simulator into an absurd racing track that could rival Trackmania, or a cops versus robbers re-enactment, or a social survival game with mayors, bankers, guards, civilians and more. Much like its predecessors, Arma 3 thrives off the plasticity of its experience, kept alive by the impressive variety of mods.

However, what if you're after the base experience? In the vanilla download, you'll find a complex, yet relatively accessible near-future military simulator in the form of a very sandy sandbox, a variety of campaign missions, and a never-ending list of developer and custom multiplayer missions, encompassing infantry and mechanical warfare. Tanks, helicopters, jets, boats, submarines, drones, scanning equipment and the usual suspects are accompanied by a seemingly endless treasure trove of gear, ranging from a simple compass to complicated infrared vehicle markers. This is a game that can adapt to almost any conflict scenario you throw at it: Ask Arma 3 to give you a high tension hostage rescue mission in close quarters urban environments, and it'll do it. Ask it to give you a gargantuan battle across enormous plains with hundreds of units and kilometres in scale, and it'll do it.

The scale isn't just for encounters. Everything from physical needles in car dashboard panels, to physically modelled bullet trajectories for every single projectile, to the flattening of grass when a vehicle passes through, is represented surprisingly faithfully for a game that was initially released in 2013. It's impressive, especially as a new player, to hop into Arma 3 and find yourself surrounded by a realistically cohesive experience.

However, this realism and detail comes at a cost. Despite the massive progress made since its predecessors, the game still suffers from major accessibility problems. Controls are better but menu navigation is strangely old-fashioned, often relying on scrolling lists rather than radial menus. A million keyboard shortcuts may be memorised by experts after hundreds of hours of play, but newcomers can find that level of demand overwhelming. Giving a simple squad order can often require scrolling through four or five different lists of nested commands, multiple methods of camera manipulation, and even still you're required to pray to RNJesus for the AI to respond. Character controls are clunky and stiff, and you'll often find yourself dying due to fumbling with the game, rather than your strategic decisions. Even on the best servers, you'll encounter strange lag and rubberbanding. Vehicle physics frequently adopt a mind of their own. And of course, you may struggle to surpass 30 FPS even on the most powerful of machines, due to the engine's ancient architecture and the nature of what's on offer.

All of the above, and tens of other examples, add up to play that can often become unpredictable and annoying. Avoid jumping back and forth from this to something like Battlefield or even Red Orchestra, because the difference may make Arma 3 unpalatable. However, the reverse might well happen: You might find yourself missing the tactical depth and dynamics from Bohemia's game instead!

You see: What makes Arma 3 and the series as a whole so special is that it requires a very different style of play. You need intel, teamwork, equipment, and thinking. You can't just jump into this game, use twitch reflexes to down everyone, and then automatically heal behind cover. You need to truly work with your peers and adapt to the circumstances, employing a level of care and precision that few games demand. The rhythms of this game's battles can be highly staccato, bouncing from eerie silence to an eruption of momentary chaos, capable of ending just as quickly as it begun. Much like the conflicts of real life that it seeks to emulate, a single well-placed shot can take you down, but so can you to your foes. This is a game where you'll need snipers perched on mountains kilometres away, tanks on the front lines, drones buzzing above relaying enemy positions, and infiltration teams flanking and sabotaging the enemy. It is that diversity and complexity of the thousand moving gears that builds a platform for warfare unlike that which any other game can provide. If you can overlook the unfortunate mountain of mechanical and technological awkwardness (and play online for the fun-enhancing teamwork with real human beings), you'll find a real diamond in the rough here.

[h1]★★★☆☆[/h1]
